newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu to attend Gabon peace summit.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu to attend Gabon peace summit.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko, battling cancer and rebel advances, flies to Gabon on Wednesday to attend a regional summit seeking peace in Zaire, but aides insisted he was not fleeing the country and would return to Kinshasa.

A government statement said Mobutu, who has dominated Zaire for over three decades, would have talks in Gabon's capital Libreville with the presidents of Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon.

The talks were a follow-up to a weekend peace summit between Mobutu, rebel leader Laurent Kabila and South Africa's Nelson Mandela on a South African ship in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire. That meeting proved inconclusive.
"The president will go to Libreville on Wednesday and will return on Friday," Mobutu spokesman Kabuya Lumuna told Reuters.
A Mobutu aide, who asked not to be named, said it would be wrong to interpret the president's departure as a flight into exile. Mobutu, he recalled, had repeatedly ruled out fleeing.
Mobutu, 66, has seen his hold over Africa's third largest nation broken by a whirlwind rebel offensive. Many in Kinshasa, hungry for change, welcome the prospect of Kabila's arrival.
Kabila and his commanders, who took up arms in October, say they are building up for a final push against the capital.
Zaire's government says its forces have counter-attacked and are battling to retake the town of Kikwit.

"We are in the process of retaking Kikwit. Intense fighting is taking place. The rebels have lost 500 men," emergency rule prime minister Likulia Bolongo's military adviser, Captain Aime Atembina, told a news conference in Kinshasa.
Independent sources confirmed a belated army counter-thrust but said the clashes were near Kenge, closer to Kinshasa.
Diplomatic sources say the front line is close to the strategic Kwango River bridge 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.

South African Vice-President Thabo Mbeki and U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson held talks in Pretoria on ways to avert a battle for Kinshasa. Mbeki later announced plans to visit Zaire and five nations in the region to keep peace talks on track.
U.N. agencies stepped up security in Kinshasa, evacuating the last non-essential staff, a senior U.N. source said.

On the humanitarian front, 1,200 Rwandan Hutu refugees who were to be airlifted home arrived safely by train in Zaire's third city of Kisangani -- the first such trip since 92 were killed in a stampede on Sunday.
The U.N. has flown home nearly 10,000 Hutus since launching the airlift on April 27 -- 1,976 of them on Tuesday.
